events.desc: Reginald Foxworth: Ah, Doily Manor! What a magnificent establishment. I was personally invited, you know — the Countess herself wrote to me. We're old friends. Very old friends. The oldest of friends, in fact.
events.thinking: The chandelier catches the light and something behind my navel opens — a pull toward the gold and crystal that has no words, just the hollowing-out of proximity to value, my fingers curling against my palms before I've noticed them moving. Then I angle my shoulder and the medal swings into the chandelier light and my spine reaches upward — not decided, arrived — stretching toward something above me that hasn't happened yet, a vertical pull that lives in my upper chest and has nothing to do with the gut's hunger for the gold overhead. Hartwell glances at the ribbon and his eyes hold there for half a second and warmth floods behind my sternum, sudden and sharp, filling the space the hollow left — seen, my breathing shifts, my jaw loosens into the warmth before the next word has formed. The room sorts itself into angles — Hartwell's reactions arrive on schedule and my shoulders carry a particular ease around him because there is nothing to brace against, but Clara's attention lands on details before mine does and something pulls taut across my chest, a different tension, she doesn't settle into the reading I'm drawing of the room and my fingertips fizz against each other tracking the angles between her gaze and the corridor and the guest book where Marsh is standing with that careful smile. The Brixton Boys watch without blinking and the back of my neck prickles — not the gut's pull, not the spine's reaching, something flatter, a surface awareness that my body handles without breaking stride because the words are already forming. My jaw opens and the words find their shape — the Countess, the invitation, the old friendship — each syllable arriving with a warmth that only fabrication gives, smooth, placed, the tongue knowing exactly where to put the weight the way my fingers knew where to place each detail of the story about the buried treasure when I was ten, building something step by step and watching the boy's eyes widen as the architecture took hold. The plan is already in the speaking and the speaking is the plan — my peripheral vision mapping the corridor to my left, the staircase beyond Marsh, the library door half-open in the distance, each angle fizzing through my fingertips while the gut's hollow pull reaches toward all of it at once, the house opening before me like something I haven't had yet but already feel the shape of in my ribs.
